chapter: Image, travel and Black, Brown and Beige
title: Playing Black, Brown and Beige with the Philadelphia Symphony at Robin Hood Dell
summary: Greer recalls performing with the orchestra, Sarah Vaughan singing Come Sunday, and that nobody recorded it.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Do you remember how the first Carnegie Hall Concert, "Black, Brown and Beige," how that came about?
No. How'd it come to be written?
No, no, how you all got the job. That was the first time you all had formally played there, 1943, Wait, I got it here. right? I think it was January. / Hold on a second. (Pause)
Now, concerning "Black, Brown and Beige," the performance of "Black, Brown and Beige," you played some -- performed it some places other than Carnegie Hall before you played the Carnegie Hall?

I think the first time we played that, we had this engagement to play with the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra, which was in my estimation one of the greatest orchestras, even more widely acclaimed than the Philharmonic in
New York. We played a place called 'Robin Hood Dell,' that's right.

leads me right-- I remember--my memory of this symphony orchestra played all of our tunes. We set in with the symphony orchestra. We were right in the middle of the symphony orchestra, 100 or so of us. And we played -- I don't know, I'm quite sure we played "Black, Brown and Beige." That's the first time Duke played it. Because the symphony orchestra was so enthused about this particular number, "Black, Brown and Beige." Of course, they played a lot of our different tunes, you know. And we had a field day, man. Can you imagine us sitting up there in the middle of this great big symphony, one of the best in the world that Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra. Don't let no one kid you. They were something else. They traveled all over the world. And this Robin Hood Dell, prettiest place, outdoors, youknow, in the summer, beautiful.

And the only thing Duke and I regretted, Duke and the boys regretted rather, nobody put it on tape or record. That was the greatest thing we ever played. The greatest. That was the greatest concert or the greatest thing we ever done. Everyone said it. And we had guys, because we recorded all the time. How they missed that, I'll never know. How they ever missed that I will never, never know.
They had a guest soloist, Ella Fitzgerald? It was either Ella Fitzgerald -- I'm sure it was Ella Fitzgerald or,
at that time, Sarah Vaughn.
Oh, yeah, because she had been working with Earl Hines at about that time, right?

She was singing like a mockingbird. I'm sure it was Sarah Vaughn. It wasn't Ella. Man, that was it. That thing, recording anybody -- nobody thought to record it. If that had been recorded, you could demand any amount of money you wanted for that, you know.
Was it broadcast?
No, no.
It wasn't broadcast, either?
No, uh-uh. Everybody slept it. It was really the Duke was -- he slept it, Irving Mills, our manager, slept it. And after it was all over we knew it should have been recorded.
You played the entire work, "Black, Brown and Beige," with the orchestra?
With the symphony orchestra. Can you imagine how that would sound, with all them violins and stuff? Man, "Come Sunday"-- and "Come Sunday" was in it.
Right.
Can you imagine them violins crying, huh? And Sarah Vaughn singing?
Yeah, because I remember when I first heard it on record, just that opening, (humming). Just that,
you know, because you play a thing on there, (humming) and when they come back with that (humming). Then it goes into something else, you know. But I know that must have been a pretty powerful --

Man, a hundred and some musicians and them strings, boy, when they played "Come Sunday," and Sarah was singing, you know, not no trills, just plain, natural singing. And she could go -- she didn't have all that frills. Just beautiful singing.
She just sang notes?
Notes.
No words? Did she have any words or did she just --
I don't recall, but I know it was pretty. And people sitting all on -- that's the prettiest place, man (of the Schuylkill River) the banks, man, the moon was shining. I don't know, man.
